Quick Jump to Document Sections
Founder's Direct POVDocument Status: V1 Product / Business Requirements · Apparel Niche

AUTONOMOUS LISTING AGENT

V1 Business Requirements & End-to-End Listing Process (Apparel / Fashion Marketplace Sellers)
Important Notice on Living Marketplace Rules
Marketplace schemas, required fields, allowed values and validation rules change. The product must therefore treat marketplace requirements as living rules rather than a one-time hard-coded field list. Amazon explicitly provides marketplace/ product-type schemas and notes that requirements can change; Flipkart likewise states that listing rules are subject to change.

Purpose of this Document

Define, in non-technical business language, exactly what the product must collect, understand, create, validate, submit, monitor, repair and report when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.

ItemDefinition
V1 product promiseSeller gives basic brand + product information once. The agent turns it into marketplace-ready listings and manages the listing lifecycle until the listing is live or a human decision is genuinely required.
Primary nicheApparel / fashion products.
Primary userD2C brands, manufacturers, traders, small sellers and marketplace agencies managing apparel catalogs.
Core outcomeOne product source of truth → marketplace-specific listing → validation → submission → error resolution → live confirmation.
Operating principleDo not ask the seller for information the system can reliably derive, reuse or validate. Ask only when missing information materially blocks a correct listing.

1. Product in One Sentence

"The Autonomous Listing Agent is a listing operations agent, not merely a content generator. It takes a seller's product information and assets, builds a canonical product record, maps that product to each marketplace's category and field structure, generates or transforms listing content, validates completeness and compliance, submits the listing, reads marketplace responses, fixes resolvable errors, asks the seller only for unresolved information, resubmits, and confirms the final live status."

2. The End-to-End Flow

The complete lifecycle from seller onboarding to live verification consists of 19 operational stages:

1
Seller / brand onboarding
Capture stable business, legal, brand & tax identity once
2
Marketplace account connection
Authenticate seller accounts, store IDs & default commercial terms
3
Product intake
Multi-modal ingestion: forms, CSV, ERP, images & size charts
4
Product understanding
Isolate verified factual data from promotional marketing noise
5
Category & sub-category classification
Map gender & apparel type into marketplace taxonomy
6
Attribute extraction & normalization
Normalize fabric, fit, pattern, color, weave & care
7
Canonical Product Intelligence record
Create immutable single source of truth record
8
Marketplace schema mapping
Transform canonical facts into target marketplace schemas
9
Content generation & optimization
Generate titles, bullets, descriptions & search keywords
10
Media and variant validation
Validate size charts, swatch shots, parent-child links
11
Compliance & completeness validation
Pre-flight checks against Legal Metrology 2022 & portal rules
12
Human clarification only where necessary
Targeted single-question prompts for blocking gaps
13
Marketplace submission
Dispatch validated payloads to marketplace APIs
14
Submission/status monitoring
Asynchronous polling & webhook listeners for feed outcomes
15
Error diagnosis
Translate raw portal error codes into plain actionable language
16
Automatic correction
Auto-fix deterministic enum mismatches, formatting & sizing
17
Resubmission
Safe bounded retry with updated payload and incremented attempt
18
Live confirmation
Capture live URL, marketplace SKU, ASIN/FSN and active state
19
Dashboard status + audit history
Show unified multi-marketplace operational view & audit trail

3. V1 Scope and Non-Goals

Definition of Success
A product is not considered 'listed' merely because a submission was sent. It is successful only when the marketplace confirms the relevant SKU/listing is live/active and the dashboard can show the marketplace identifier, current status and latest validation state.
In V1 ScopeNot the Primary V1 Objective
Apparel product listingFull marketplace order management
Multi-marketplace listing from one dashboardFull inventory/warehouse management
Product/category/attribute understandingAdvertising optimization
Title, bullets, description, keywords and structured attributesPricing optimization as a standalone agent
Variant and media handlingReturns/reconciliation as a standalone workflow
Validation, error interpretation and correctionCustomer service automation
Listing status and historyEnd-to-end marketplace business operating system

4. Marketplace Strategy

V1 should be designed around a common apparel product model plus marketplace-specific adapters. The common model is the source of truth. Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are required, optional, conditionally required, allowed values, formatting rules, variation rules and submission/status behavior.

  • Target marketplace set: Can include Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, AJIO, Meesho and Nykaa Fashion, subject to the commercial/API access available to the business.
  • Category Semantic Variance: Do not assume that the same apparel category means the same thing on every marketplace.
  • No Hard-Coded Lists: Do not hard-code a single universal 'required fields' list.
  • Dynamic Schemas: For each connected marketplace, the product should maintain a current marketplace/category schema and map the canonical product into it.
  • Amazon Documentation: Amazon's current developer documentation describes Product Type Definitions as the source for product-type and marketplace requirements, including required/conditional attributes.
  • Flipkart Documentation: Flipkart's official Listing Management documentation similarly separates product information from the seller listing and states that listing rules can change, so errors should be handled explicitly.

5.3 Seller Catalog Intake Options

The seller should be able to provide product information in multiple ways:

  • Single product form.
  • Bulk spreadsheet/template upload.
  • Images + basic product information.
  • Existing catalog export.
  • ERP/PIM/catalog source, where available.
  • URL/website product page, where permitted.
  • Combination of the above.
Data Ingestion Rule
The system should merge these inputs rather than forcing the seller to repeat information.

7. Variants: The Product Family Model

The system must distinguish the product style from the sellable variant. A common apparel family is one style with multiple colors and sizes.

LevelExampleRule
Parent / styleTSHIRT-001Represents the underlying product/style.
Color childTSHIRT-001-BLKOne color variation.
Size childTSHIRT-001-BLK-MOne sellable size/color combination.
Marketplace listingMarketplace-specific SKU/listing IDExternal representation of the sellable item.

Core Variation Invariants

  • Store a complete size × color matrix, including unavailable combinations.
  • Never silently create a variant that the seller did not provide.
  • Keep seller SKU stable even if marketplace identifiers differ.
  • Record parent-child relationships separately from marketplace-specific variation rules.
  • Amazon's listing schema explicitly distinguishes parent and child listing levels, with different attributes applicable to each.

8. Media / Image Intake

For apparel, image requirements can differ by marketplace. Amazon's current seller guidance, for example, describes a main image for parent and child listings and allows alternative images for details such as fabric, features and angles.

9. Content Intelligence Layer

This is the content layer shown in the reference architecture. The agent should not generate copy from images alone when authoritative product facts are available elsewhere.

Content ObjectPurposeSource / Rule
Marketplace titleCustomer-facing product titleCanonical facts + marketplace title rules
Key features / bulletsFast communication of product benefits/featuresVerified product facts only
DescriptionDetailed customer-facing descriptionCanonical facts + category context
Search keywordsSearch discoverabilityRelevant terms grounded in product/category; avoid unsupported claims
Backend/search fieldsMarketplace-specific search metadataMarketplace schema
Size/fit informationReduce size uncertaintyBrand size data; never invent measurements

ClaimsUSP/performance statementsMust be supported by seller-provided evidence
Golden Rule for AI Content
The agent may transform, structure and improve verified information. It must not invent fabric composition, measurements, certifications, performance claims, care instructions, country of origin, tax information, or other factual attributes simply to complete a listing.

10. Canonical Product Intelligence Layer

For every product, maintain one canonical record that becomes the source of truth before any marketplace-specific output is created.

11.1 Source-of-Truth Priority

  1. Seller-provided structured data.
  2. Seller-provided documents/labels/size charts and authoritative product assets.
  3. Connected catalog/PIM/ERP data, if explicitly connected and trusted.
  4. Existing marketplace data, when it is the seller's own authoritative listing data.
  5. Derived values from deterministic normalization or category rules.
  6. AI-generated inference only when the field is non-critical and the inference is clearly permitted.
  7. Never use an AI guess to fill a critical factual/compliance field.

12. Step-by-Step Autonomous Listing Workflow

STEP 1

UNDERSTAND PRODUCT

Goal: Build a complete understanding of the product before generating a marketplace listing.

Inputs: Seller form, spreadsheet, images, website/catalog data, size chart, product documents and connected systems.

Actions: Identify product and variants; separate facts from marketing language; detect missing/conflicting/duplicate data; determine reliable vs confirmation-needed facts.

Output: Structured product facts with source and confidence.

STEP 2

CLASSIFY

Goal: Decide the correct product category and sub-category for each marketplace.

Actions: Identify product type (T-shirt, shirt, dress, jeans, etc.); identify audience/gender; map canonical product to marketplace taxonomy; verify seller category eligibility; use evidence & rules (no random guesses).

Output: Canonical category + marketplace-specific category/product type + confidence.

STEP 3

EXTRACT ATTRIBUTES

Goal: Populate all product attributes from the available evidence.

Actions: Extract color, size, fabric, fit, pattern, neckline, sleeve, length, closure, occasion; normalize synonyms into controlled values; preserve original seller value + normalized value; track source; detect contradictions (e.g., '100% cotton' vs 'cotton-poly blend').

Output: Complete canonical attribute set with missing/conflicting fields identified.

STEP 4

FILL MARKETPLACE SCHEMA

Goal: Transform the canonical product into the exact field structure expected by each selected marketplace.

Actions: Load current marketplace/category schema; map canonical fields to portal fields; apply allowed-value enums; mark required, conditional, optional and unsupported fields; build parent/child variation structure; map media roles and content fields.

Output: Marketplace-ready draft for each marketplace.

STEP 5

GENERATE CONTENT

Goal: Create customer-facing listing content from verified product facts.

Create: Title, bullets/key features, description, search keywords, size/fit copy, portal-specific content fields.

Rules: No unsupported claims; no invented specs; do not copy prohibited content; keep consistent factual identity while adapting tone/format to marketplace rules.

Output: Content package with source traceability.

STEP 6

VALIDATE

Goal: Catch problems before marketplace submission.

Validate Checklist: Required fields present; allowed values; parent/child relationship valid; color & size consistency; image presence & association; price/MRP consistency; product identifier rules; HSN/tax fields; country of origin & manufacturer details; content policy checks; no conflicting facts.

Output: PASS, BLOCKED, or NEEDS HUMAN INPUT with field-level reasons.

STEP 7

FIND MISSING DATA

Goal: Determine whether missing information can be recovered automatically.

Try in this strict hierarchy:

  1. Existing canonical product record.
  2. Same brand's trusted catalog conventions.
  3. Connected PIM/ERP/catalog.
  4. Existing marketplace listing owned by the seller.
  5. Seller-provided files/assets.
  6. Deterministic category mapping.
  7. Ask seller.

Output: Missing fields reduced to the smallest set genuinely required.

STEP 8

ASK HUMAN ONLY WHEN NECESSARY

Goal: Ask the seller one clear question instead of sending them back to a large form.

Examples: 'What is the fabric composition: 100% cotton or 95% cotton / 5% elastane?', 'Please provide the size chart for this product.', 'Which MRP should be used for the black variant?', 'Please confirm whether this is a women\'s or unisex product.'

Question Must Include: Why information is required; which products/variants it affects; exact expected answer; optional safe suggestions.

Post-Response: Update canonical record and resume automatically from blocked step.

STEP 9

SUBMIT

Goal: Send the validated listing to the selected marketplace(s).

Actions: Submit only required and permitted fields; record submission time and job ID/reference; store exact version submitted; update status from Draft/Ready to Submitted/Pending.

Output: Marketplace submission record.

STEP 10

CHECK STATUS

Goal: Determine what happened after submission.

Possible Outcomes: Accepted/processing · Active/live · Rejected · Partially accepted · Missing information · Validation failure · Pending marketplace review · Account/category permission issue.

Rule: Keep checking until a terminal state is reached or a human action is required.

STEP 11

FIX ERRORS

Goal: Diagnose and resolve errors without making the seller repeat the process.

For every error: Capture error code/message; identify affected SKU/field; translate to plain language; determine if auto-fixable; apply deterministic fix; revalidate.

Auto-Fixable Classes: Wrong portal enum mapped from known canonical value; formatting issue; safely calculable derived field; incorrect parent/child mapping.

Human-Required Classes: Missing factual product info; conflicting seller data; brand authorization/approval; account issue; compliance evidence request.

STEP 12

RESUBMIT

Goal: Send the corrected listing back to the marketplace.

Actions: Keep same seller SKU/identity; record correction made; increment submission attempt count; submit only after validation passes; preserve failed versions for audit.

STEP 13

CONFIRM LIVE

Goal: Confirm the product is genuinely sellable/live.

Minimum Confirmation: Status = live/active; marketplace ID captured; seller SKU mapped; variant status captured; live URL captured where available; latest successful sync timestamp recorded.

Output: LIVE status.

STEP 14

SHOW DASHBOARD STATUS

Goal: Give the seller a simple operational view.

Show: Overall status; per-marketplace status; current step; issue count; human actions required; last sync; marketplace listing ID/SKU; live URL; attempt history.

Core Dashboard Mandate
The dashboard should answer: "What is live, what is not live, why, and what do I need to do?"

13. Listing Status Model

The product tracks granular operational status across all lifecycle phases:

StatusMeaningSeller Action

14.2 Product Detail View

The detail view must render ten dedicated inspector panels:

  • Canonical product information: Core attributes, fabric, weave, care, and legal declarations.
  • Variants and size/color matrix: Interactive matrix of all styles, colorways, and sizes.
  • Images and media validation: Slot mapping, aspect ratio check, background validation.
  • Generated content: Marketplace-specific title, bullets, search terms, and description.
  • Marketplace-specific preview/mapped fields: Side-by-side view of portal payloads.
  • Validation results: Rule-by-rule pass/fail scorecard with severity flags.
  • Marketplace status cards: Status badge, external listing ID, live portal link, last sync.
  • Open issues and required actions: Human action items with exact questions and input fields.
  • Submission attempts: Historic payload snapshots, timestamps, and error responses.
  • Change history / audit trail: Complete record of who/what modified any field.

15. Error Management Framework

Error ClassExampleAgent Behavior
Missing dataFabric composition absentFind source → if unavailable, ask seller
Invalid valueMarketplace does not accept seller's color termMap to allowed marketplace value
Category mismatchProduct mapped to wrong product typeReclassify and remap
Variation errorSize/color relationship invalidRebuild mapping from canonical variant matrix
Media errorImage not acceptedIdentify failed image rule; replace/remap if possible
Content errorTitle/field violates marketplace ruleRewrite using verified facts
Identifier errorGTIN/identifier issueAsk seller / use approved exemption flow if applicable
Compliance errorRequired declaration missingRequest exact compliance information
Account permissionSeller not approved for category/brandCreate human action task
Marketplace outage/technicalSubmission unavailableRetry according to safe retry policy; do not create duplicates
Unknown errorUnrecognized marketplace messageStop unsafe automation, show raw message + plain-language summary, create human task

15.1 Error Resolution Loop

  1. Capture error exactly as returned.
  2. Normalize it into an internal error category.
  3. Identify affected field/variant/listing.
  4. Determine whether the error is deterministic and safely fixable.
  5. Apply fix if safe.
  6. Re-run validation.
  7. Resubmit.
  8. If still failing, stop repeated retries and escalate.
  9. Show the seller the exact remaining action.
Important Anti-Loop Rule
The agent must never repeatedly submit the same failed listing indefinitely. Every retry needs a changed input, a known retryable condition, or a marketplace status transition that justifies another attempt.

16. Human-in-the-Loop Rules

The product should be autonomous by default, but not reckless. Human involvement is a controlled exception.

Ask the Seller WhenDo NOT Ask When
A critical factual field is genuinely missing.The answer already exists in the canonical record.
Two authoritative sources conflict.The value can be deterministically normalized.
Marketplace requires seller-specific approval/evidence.The agent can safely transform an existing value.
A compliance declaration cannot be verified.The missing value is merely a formatting variation.
A category/brand permission decision is required.The marketplace has a known mapping for the category.

18. Apparel Compliance Data to Capture

This section is a business-data checklist, not legal advice. The product should capture the data and avoid assuming legal compliance merely because fields are populated.

Compliance DataCapture AtNotes
Manufacturer name/addressBrand + productExact legal details where applicable
Marketer/brand owner detailsBrand/productWhere applicable
Importer detailsProductFor imported products where applicable
Country of origin/manufactureProductDo not infer from brand location
Consumer care contactBrandEmail/phone as applicable
Size declarationVariant/productInternational size + metric measurements where required
MRP inclusive of taxesVariant/productCapture exact seller-declared MRP
Fabric/fiber compositionProductCapture exact composition rather than generic material wording
Care instructionsProductSeller/manufacturer-provided
Package declarationsProduct/packageWhere applicable
HSN/tax classificationVariant/productSeller-provided/verified; do not blindly infer final tax classification
Legal Metrology Garment Amendment (2022)
India's Department of Consumer Affairs has specific garment-related Legal Metrology requirements. Its 2022 amendment states that certain garment/hosiery sales require declarations including manufacturer/marketer/brand owner/importer details, consumer-care contact, size, MRP and that the information be displayed on an e-commerce website. General packaged-commodity rules also cover declarations such as manufacturer/packer/importer, country of origin, generic name, net quantity, MRP and consumer care.

19. Marketplace-Specific Requirement Matrix

Use this matrix as the product design framework. Exact field names and required/conditional status should come from the current marketplace/category schema at the time of listing.

MarketplaceCommon Apparel Data to ExpectDesign Requirement
AmazonProduct type, brand, title, identifiers/exemption, color, size, material/fabric, department/gender, bullets, description, images, variation structure, compliance/product detailsUse current Product Type Definition for marketplace + product type. Requirements can be conditional and can change.
FlipkartProduct/vertical attributes, brand, category, color/size, product description, images, MRP/selling price, package dimensions/weight, HSN and listing/fulfillment fieldsSeparate product identity from seller listing/commercial attributes; preserve listing status and seller SKU mapping.

22. V1 Acceptance Criteria

  • A seller can create a brand profile once and reuse it across products.
  • A seller can provide apparel product information through a structured form or bulk input.
  • The system can represent one style with multiple color/size variants.
  • Every important canonical attribute can retain its source and confidence.
  • The system can map one canonical product into marketplace-specific category/field structures.
  • The system can distinguish required, conditional, optional and unsupported fields.
  • The system can generate title, bullets, description and keywords from verified product facts.
  • The system can validate the product before submission and show blocking reasons.
  • The system can identify missing data and ask targeted human questions.
  • The system can submit a listing and record the submission attempt.
  • The system can read the resulting marketplace status/error.
  • The system can automatically fix defined deterministic error classes.
  • The system can retry safely without creating uncontrolled duplicate submissions.
  • The system can escalate unresolved issues to a human.
  • The system can confirm a listing as LIVE only after marketplace success confirmation.
  • The dashboard can show per-marketplace status, listing identifiers, issues and latest activity.
  • The system preserves history so the team can understand what changed and why.

23. Product Metrics for V1

MetricDefinition
Time to first listingTime from complete product intake to first successful live listing.
Listing success ratePercentage of listing jobs that reach LIVE without manual marketplace intervention.
First-pass success ratePercentage of submissions accepted without a correction cycle.
Auto-resolution ratePercentage of errors resolved by the agent without seller intervention.
Human question ratePercentage of products requiring at least one seller question.
Average human questions per SKUQuestions asked per product/job.
Error recurrence ratePercentage of issues that reappear after correction.
Duplicate submission rateUnwanted duplicate listing/submission incidents.
Attribute completenessPercentage of required/conditional fields correctly populated before submission.
Live confirmation accuracyPercentage of listings marked LIVE that are actually live.

24. Handoff to Lead Engineer: What Must Be Clear Before Build

  • Canonical product is the source of truth; marketplace listings are derived representations.
  • Marketplace schemas are versioned and can change.
  • Every field should have a source, and critical facts should have confidence/evidence.
  • Required fields are marketplace + category + context dependent.
  • Variant relationships are first-class product data, not just a UI feature.
  • Listing status is per marketplace and per variant where necessary.
  • Errors are first-class records with classification, severity and resolution state.
  • Human questions are first-class workflow tasks, not generic support tickets.
  • Every submission and correction should be auditable.
  • The workflow must be resumable. If a seller answers one question, the agent continues from the blocked step rather than restarting the entire job.
  • The agent must be idempotent at the business level: repeated status checks or safe retries should not create duplicate product identities.
  • Preserve separation: The system should preserve marketplace-specific data without polluting the canonical product with marketplace-only fields.

Content languageStart with English; keep the content model language-ready.
Image generationDo not make image generation a dependency for V1 listing completion.
Marketplace schema refreshTreat schema/rules as versioned and refreshable rather than static.
Error libraryBuild an internal error taxonomy and continuously map marketplace errors into it.
Confidence thresholdDefine which attributes can be inferred and which always require evidence/confirmation.
Bulk listingDesign for one SKU and bulk SKU jobs from the same underlying workflow.

  • Amazon Selling Partner API — Manage Product Listings: https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/lang-en_EN/docs/manage-product-listings-guide
  • Amazon India Seller Central — apparel image guidance / seller listing guidance: https://sellercentral.amazon.in/
  • Flipkart Seller API — Listing Management API: https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/listing-api-docs/LMAPIOverview.html
  • Flipkart Seller API — Marketplace platform overview: https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/FMPlatOverview.html

Step-by-Step Autonomous Listing Workflow STEP 1 ### UNDERSTAND PRODUCT **Goal:** Build a complete understanding of the product before generating a marketplace listing. **Inputs:** Seller form, spreadsheet, images, website/catalog data, size chart, product documents and connected systems. **Actions:** Identify product and variants; separate facts from marketing language; detect missing/conflicting/duplicate data; determine reliable vs confirmation-needed facts. **Output:** Structured product facts with source and confidence. STEP 2 ### CLASSIFY **Goal:** Decide the correct product category and sub-category for each marketplace. **Actions:** Identify product type (T-shirt, shirt, dress, jeans, etc.); identify audience/gender; map canonical product to marketplace taxonomy; verify seller category eligibility; use evidence & rules (no random guesses). **Output:** Canonical category + marketplace-specific category/product type + confidence. STEP 3 ### EXTRACT ATTRIBUTES **Goal:** Populate all product attributes from the available evidence. **Actions:** Extract color, size, fabric, fit, pattern, neckline, sleeve, length, closure, occasion; normalize synonyms into controlled values; preserve original seller value + normalized value; track source; detect contradictions (e.g., '100% cotton' vs 'cotton-poly blend'). **Output:** Complete canonical attribute set with missing/conflicting fields identified. STEP 4 ### FILL MARKETPLACE SCHEMA **Goal:** Transform the canonical product into the exact field structure expected by each selected marketplace. **Actions:** Load current marketplace/category schema; map canonical fields to portal fields; apply allowed-value enums; mark required, conditional, optional and unsupported fields; build parent/child variation structure; map media roles and content fields. **Output:** Marketplace-ready draft for each marketplace. STEP 5 ### GENERATE CONTENT **Goal:** Create customer-facing listing content from verified product facts. **Create:** Title, bullets/key features, description, search keywords, size/fit copy, portal-specific content fields. **Rules:** No unsupported claims; no invented specs; do not copy prohibited content; keep consistent factual identity while adapting tone/format to marketplace rules. **Output:** Content package with source traceability. STEP 6 ### VALIDATE **Goal:** Catch problems before marketplace submission. **Validate Checklist:** Required fields present; allowed values; parent/child relationship valid; color & size consistency; image presence & association; price/MRP consistency; product identifier rules; HSN/tax fields; country of origin & manufacturer details; content policy checks; no conflicting facts. **Output:** `PASS`, `BLOCKED`, or `NEEDS HUMAN INPUT` with field-level reasons. STEP 7 ### FIND MISSING DATA **Goal:** Determine whether missing information can be recovered automatically. **Try in this strict hierarchy:** 1. Existing canonical product record. 2. Same brand's trusted catalog conventions. 3. Connected PIM/ERP/catalog. 4. Existing marketplace listing owned by the seller. 5. Seller-provided files/assets. 6. Deterministic category mapping. 7. Ask seller. **Output:** Missing fields reduced to the smallest set genuinely required. STEP 8 ### ASK HUMAN ONLY WHEN NECESSARY **Goal:** Ask the seller one clear question instead of sending them back to a large form. **Examples:** _'What is the fabric composition: 100% cotton or 95% cotton / 5% elastane?'_, _'Please provide the size chart for this product.'_, _'Which MRP should be used for the black variant?'_, _'Please confirm whether this is a women\\'s or unisex product.'_ **Question Must Include:** Why information is required; which products/variants it affects; exact expected answer; optional safe suggestions. **Post-Response:** Update canonical record and resume automatically from blocked step. STEP 9 ### SUBMIT **Goal:** Send the validated listing to the selected marketplace(s). **Actions:** Submit only required and permitted fields; record submission time and job ID/reference; store exact version submitted; update status from Draft/Ready to Submitted/Pending. **Output:** Marketplace submission record. STEP 10 ### CHECK STATUS **Goal:** Determine what happened after submission. **Possible Outcomes:** Accepted/processing · Active/live · Rejected · Partially accepted · Missing information · Validation failure · Pending marketplace review · Account/category permission issue. **Rule:** Keep checking until a terminal state is reached or a human action is required. STEP 11 ### FIX ERRORS **Goal:** Diagnose and resolve errors without making the seller repeat the process. **For every error:** Capture error code/message; identify affected SKU/field; translate to plain language; determine if auto-fixable; apply deterministic fix; revalidate. **Auto-Fixable Classes:** Wrong portal enum mapped from known canonical value; formatting issue; safely calculable derived field; incorrect parent/child mapping. **Human-Required Classes:** Missing factual product info; conflicting seller data; brand authorization/approval; account issue; compliance evidence request. STEP 12 ### RESUBMIT **Goal:** Send the corrected listing back to the marketplace. **Actions:** Keep same seller SKU/identity; record correction made; increment submission attempt count; submit only after validation passes; preserve failed versions for audit. STEP 13 ### CONFIRM LIVE **Goal:** Confirm the product is genuinely sellable/live. **Minimum Confirmation:** Status = live/active; marketplace ID captured; seller SKU mapped; variant status captured; live URL captured where available; latest successful sync timestamp recorded. **Output:** `LIVE` status. STEP 14 ### SHOW DASHBOARD STATUS **Goal:** Give the seller a simple operational view. **Show:** Overall status; per-marketplace status; current step; issue count; human actions required; last sync; marketplace listing ID/SKU; live URL; attempt history. Core Dashboard Mandate The dashboard should answer: _"What is live, what is not live, why, and what do I need to do?"_ ## 13\. Listing Status Model The product tracks granular operational status across all lifecycle phases: Status Meaning Seller Action `DRAFT` Product information has been started but is not ready. Provide missing information if shown. `UNDERSTANDING` Agent is interpreting product inputs. None `CLASSIFYING` Agent is selecting category/product type. None unless ambiguous. `READY_FOR_REVIEW` Draft is structurally ready but requires seller confirmation. Review only if requested by workflow. `READY_TO_LIST` Validation passed for selected marketplace(s). None `SUBMITTING` Listing is being sent. None `PROCESSING` Marketplace is processing the submission. None `LIVE` Marketplace confirmed the listing is active/live. None `PARTIALLY_LIVE` Some variants/marketplaces are live while others are not. Resolve failed portions if needed. `BLOCKED` Required information/permission/compliance issue prevents progress. Complete the displayed task. `ERROR` Submission/validation failed. Usually none if auto-fix is possible; otherwise resolve task. `HUMAN_ACTION_REQUIRED` Agent cannot safely proceed without seller input/action. Answer the exact question or perform the requested marketplace action. `PAUSED` Seller or system intentionally paused the listing. Resume when ready. `ARCHIVED` Listing workflow is closed. None ## 14\. Dashboard Requirements ### 14.1 Product List View Column What it Should Show **Product** Product name + primary image **SKU** Seller SKU **Category** Canonical category **Variants** Count and variant summary **Amazon** Status + listing ID **Flipkart** Status + listing ID **Myntra** Status + listing ID **AJIO** Status + listing ID **Meesho** Status + listing ID **Nykaa Fashion** Status + listing ID **Overall** Live / Partial / Blocked / Error / Processing **Issues** Open issue count **Last activity** Latest workflow event ### 14.2 Product Detail View The detail view must render ten dedicated inspector panels: * **Canonical product information:** Core attributes, fabric, weave, care, and legal declarations. * **Variants and size/color matrix:** Interactive matrix of all styles, colorways, and sizes. * **Images and media validation:** Slot mapping, aspect ratio check, background validation. * **Generated content:** Marketplace-specific title, bullets, search terms, and description. * **Marketplace-specific preview/mapped fields:** Side-by-side view of portal payloads. * **Validation results:** Rule-by-rule pass/fail scorecard with severity flags. * **Marketplace status cards:** Status badge, external listing ID, live portal link, last sync. * **Open issues and required actions:** Human action items with exact questions and input fields. * **Submission attempts:** Historic payload snapshots, timestamps, and error responses. * **Change history / audit trail:** Complete record of who/what modified any field. ## 15\. Error Management Framework Error Class Example Agent Behavior **Missing data** Fabric composition absent Find source → if unavailable, ask seller **Invalid value** Marketplace does not accept seller's color term Map to allowed marketplace value **Category mismatch** Product mapped to wrong product type Reclassify and remap **Variation error** Size/color relationship invalid Rebuild mapping from canonical variant matrix **Media error** Image not accepted Identify failed image rule; replace/remap if possible **Content error** Title/field violates marketplace rule Rewrite using verified facts **Identifier error** GTIN/identifier issue Ask seller / use approved exemption flow if applicable **Compliance error** Required declaration missing Request exact compliance information **Account permission** Seller not approved for category/brand Create human action task **Marketplace outage/technical** Submission unavailable Retry according to safe retry policy; do not create duplicates **Unknown error** Unrecognized marketplace message Stop unsafe automation, show raw message + plain-language summary, create human task ### 15.1 Error Resolution Loop 27. Capture error exactly as returned. 28. Normalize it into an internal error category. 29. Identify affected field/variant/listing. 30. Determine whether the error is deterministic and safely fixable. 31. Apply fix if safe. 32. Re-run validation. 33. Resubmit. 34. If still failing, stop repeated retries and escalate. 35. Show the seller the exact remaining action. Important Anti-Loop Rule The agent must never repeatedly submit the same failed listing indefinitely. Every retry needs a changed input, a known retryable condition, or a marketplace status transition that justifies another attempt. ## 16\. Human-in-the-Loop Rules The product should be autonomous by default, but not reckless. Human involvement is a controlled exception. Ask the Seller When Do NOT Ask When A critical factual field is genuinely missing. The answer already exists in the canonical record. Two authoritative sources conflict. The value can be deterministically normalized. Marketplace requires seller-specific approval/evidence. The agent can safely transform an existing value. A compliance declaration cannot be verified. The missing value is merely a formatting variation. A category/brand permission decision is required. The marketplace has a known mapping for the category. ## 17\. Quality Gates Before Submission Gate Pass Condition **Identity** Brand, product type and seller SKU are coherent. **Classification** Marketplace category/product type selected with sufficient confidence. **Attributes** All required/conditional attributes are populated with valid values. **Variants** Every sellable variant has consistent identity, size/color and required identifiers. **Media** Required media exists and is associated correctly. **Content** Title/bullets/description/keywords are based on verified facts and marketplace rules. **Compliance** Required product/packaging declarations and seller information are available where applicable. **Commercial** MRP/price and other required commercial fields are internally consistent. **Submission** No known blocking validation issue remains. ## 18\. Apparel Compliance Data to Capture This section is a business-data checklist, not legal advice. The product should capture the data and avoid assuming legal compliance merely because fields are populated. Compliance Data Capture At Notes **Manufacturer name/address** Brand + product Exact legal details where applicable **Marketer/brand owner details** Brand/product Where applicable **Importer details** Product For imported products where applicable **Country of origin/manufacture** Product Do not infer from brand location **Consumer care contact** Brand Email/phone as applicable **Size declaration** Variant/product International size + metric measurements where required **MRP inclusive of taxes** Variant/product Capture exact seller-declared MRP **Fabric/fiber composition** Product Capture exact composition rather than generic material wording **Care instructions** Product Seller/manufacturer-provided **Package declarations** Product/package Where applicable **HSN/tax classification** Variant/product Seller-provided/verified; do not blindly infer final tax classification Legal Metrology Garment Amendment (2022) India's Department of Consumer Affairs has specific garment-related Legal Metrology requirements. Its 2022 amendment states that certain garment/hosiery sales require declarations including manufacturer/marketer/brand owner/importer details, consumer-care contact, size, MRP and that the information be displayed on an e-commerce website. General packaged-commodity rules also cover declarations such as manufacturer/packer/importer, country of origin, generic name, net quantity, MRP and consumer care. ## 19\. Marketplace-Specific Requirement Matrix Use this matrix as the product design framework. Exact field names and required/conditional status should come from the current marketplace/category schema at the time of listing. Marketplace Common Apparel Data to Expect Design Requirement **Amazon** Product type, brand, title, identifiers/exemption, color, size, material/fabric, department/gender, bullets, description, images, variation structure, compliance/product details Use current Product Type Definition for marketplace + product type. Requirements can be conditional and can change. **Flipkart** Product/vertical attributes, brand, category, color/size, product description, images, MRP/selling price, package dimensions/weight, HSN and listing/fulfillment fields Separate product identity from seller listing/commercial attributes; preserve listing status and seller SKU mapping. **Myntra** Fashion-specific catalog/category attributes, brand, style/product details, variants, size/color, media, descriptions and seller-specific commercial/catalog information Maintain a marketplace-specific category template/schema and do not assume Amazon/Flipkart field names are portable. **AJIO** Fashion catalog attributes, category/sub-category, brand, size/color, material, media, descriptions and seller/commercial information Maintain a marketplace-specific schema and validation layer. **Meesho** Catalog/product information, category, attributes, size/color/variants, images, pricing and seller details Maintain marketplace-specific allowed values and catalog rules. **Nykaa Fashion** Product/category information, brand, attributes, media, size/color and seller/compliance information Maintain marketplace-specific schema and content rules. Nykaa's seller terms require listing information to be complete, accurate, non-misleading and compliant with applicable laws/rules. Engineering & Product Invariant **The canonical product model should be broad. Marketplace adapters should be narrow.** Never redesign the canonical product every time a marketplace introduces a new field. ## 20\. Master Field Dictionary: Minimum V1 Columns This is the recommended spreadsheet-style column set for the initial apparel catalog intake. It can be presented to sellers as a simple template, while the dashboard can hide fields that are not relevant to the selected category. Section Column / Field Requirement Business Meaning identity `seller_sku` Yes Unique seller SKU identity `parent_style_id` If variants Style/family identifier identity `product_name` Yes Seller's factual product/style name identity `brand_name` Yes Brand identity `manufacturer_name` Usually yes Manufacturer identity `manufacturer_address` Usually yes Legal address identity `product_identifier_type` If applicable GTIN/EAN/UPC etc. identity `product_identifier` If applicable Identifier value classification `gender` Category dependent Men/Women/Unisex/Boys/Girls classification `category` Yes Canonical category classification `sub_category` Yes Canonical sub-category classification `product_type` Yes Specific product type attributes `color_name` Yes Seller color attributes `normalized_color` System Normalized value attributes `size_name` Yes for sized apparel Seller size attributes `normalized_size` System Normalized value attributes `size_system` If applicable Brand/marketplace size system attributes `fit` Category dependent Slim/regular/relaxed etc. attributes `pattern` Category dependent Solid/printed/etc. attributes `fabric_type` Usually yes Cotton/denim/linen etc. attributes `fiber_composition` Critical Exact composition where available attributes `lining` If applicable Lined/unlined + material attributes `stretch` If applicable Stretch/non-stretch attributes `neckline` If applicable Crew/V/etc. attributes `collar_type` If applicable Collar attributes `sleeve_type` If applicable Sleeve attributes `sleeve_length` If applicable Sleeve length attributes `garment_length` If applicable Length attributes `rise` Bottomwear High/mid/low attributes `leg_style` Bottomwear Straight/wide/tapered etc. attributes `closure` If applicable Zip/button/pull-on attributes `pocket_type` If applicable Pocket details attributes `occasion` If applicable Casual/formal/etc. attributes `season` If applicable Seasonality care `wash_care` Usually yes Care instructions care `iron_care` If applicable Ironing instructions compliance `country_of_origin` Yes where applicable Origin compliance `mrp` Yes MRP inclusive of taxes where applicable compliance `consumer_care_email` Yes where applicable Consumer care compliance `consumer_care_phone` Yes where applicable Consumer care compliance `hsn_code` Marketplace dependent Seller-provided/verified commercial `selling_price` Marketplace dependent Selling price commercial `tax_rate` Marketplace dependent Seller-provided/verified commercial `package_weight` If required Packed weight commercial `package_length_cm` If required Package length commercial `package_breadth_cm` If required Package breadth commercial `package_height_cm` If required Package height media `main_image` Yes Main image media `additional_images` As available Additional images media `size_chart` If applicable Size chart content `title` System/generated + editable Marketplace title content `bullet_1_to_n` System-generated Key features content `description` System-generated Description content `keywords` System-generated Search terms where supported marketplace `marketplace_category` Per marketplace Mapped category marketplace `marketplace_product_type` Per marketplace Mapped product type marketplace `marketplace_sku` Per marketplace External/seller marketplace SKU marketplace `marketplace_listing_id` Per marketplace External listing ID marketplace `marketplace_status` Per marketplace Current state marketplace `live_url` Per marketplace Live URL if available workflow `overall_status` System Current overall status workflow `open_issue_count` System Open issues workflow `human_action_required` System Yes/No workflow `last_updated` System Timestamp ## 21\. Example: One Apparel Product Through the System Product Specification Case Study **Product:** Women's relaxed-fit cotton T-shirt, Black, sizes S/M/L/XL, seller SKU `FSH-TEE-001`. Stage What Happens **Intake** Seller provides SKU, product images, product name, brand, fabric composition, colors, sizes, MRP, care instructions and size chart. **Understand** Agent identifies a women's T-shirt, black color, relaxed fit, cotton composition and four sizes. **Classify** Agent maps the product to the appropriate apparel/T-shirt category for each selected marketplace. **Extract** Agent normalizes 'Jet Black' to the marketplace's accepted black value where appropriate, while preserving the seller value. **Canonical** One product record contains identity, attributes, variants, media, compliance and content. **Generate** Agent creates title, bullets, description and relevant keywords using only verified facts. **Validate** Checks all marketplace-specific mandatory/conditional fields and variant/media rules. **Human** If a marketplace requires a missing fabric detail, the agent asks one targeted question. **Submit** Agent submits the marketplace-specific representation. **Error** Marketplace rejects one size because the size value is invalid. Agent maps the canonical size to the accepted marketplace value and revalidates. **Resubmit** Corrected listing is submitted. **Live** Marketplace confirms the listing active. Listing ID and URL are stored. **Dashboard** Product shows LIVE for that marketplace and separate statuses for any other marketplaces still processing. ## 22\. V1 Acceptance Criteria * A seller can create a brand profile once and reuse it across products. * A seller can provide apparel product information through a structured form or bulk input. * The system can represent one style with multiple color/size variants. * Every important canonical attribute can retain its source and confidence. * The system can map one canonical product into marketplace-specific category/field structures. * The system can distinguish required, conditional, optional and unsupported fields. * The system can generate title, bullets, description and keywords from verified product facts. * The system can validate the product before submission and show blocking reasons. * The system can identify missing data and ask targeted human questions. * The system can submit a listing and record the submission attempt. * The system can read the resulting marketplace status/error. * The system can automatically fix defined deterministic error classes. * The system can retry safely without creating uncontrolled duplicate submissions. * The system can escalate unresolved issues to a human. * The system can confirm a listing as LIVE only after marketplace success confirmation. * The dashboard can show per-marketplace status, listing identifiers, issues and latest activity. * The system preserves history so the team can understand what changed and why. ## 23\. Product Metrics for V1 Metric Definition **Time to first listing** Time from complete product intake to first successful live listing. **Listing success rate** Percentage of listing jobs that reach LIVE without manual marketplace intervention. **First-pass success rate** Percentage of submissions accepted without a correction cycle. **Auto-resolution rate** Percentage of errors resolved by the agent without seller intervention. **Human question rate** Percentage of products requiring at least one seller question. **Average human questions per SKU** Questions asked per product/job. **Error recurrence rate** Percentage of issues that reappear after correction. **Duplicate submission rate** Unwanted duplicate listing/submission incidents. **Attribute completeness** Percentage of required/conditional fields correctly populated before submission. **Live confirmation accuracy** Percentage of listings marked LIVE that are actually live. ## 24\. Handoff to Lead Engineer: What Must Be Clear Before Build * **Canonical product is the source of truth;** marketplace listings are derived representations. * **Marketplace schemas are versioned and can change.** * **Every field should have a source**, and critical facts should have confidence/evidence. * **Required fields are marketplace + category + context dependent.** * **Variant relationships are first-class product data**, not just a UI feature. * **Listing status is per marketplace** and per variant where necessary. * **Errors are first-class records** with classification, severity and resolution state. * **Human questions are first-class workflow tasks**, not generic support tickets. * **Every submission and correction should be auditable.** * **The workflow must be resumable.** If a seller answers one question, the agent continues from the blocked step rather than restarting the entire job. * **The agent must be idempotent at the business level:** repeated status checks or safe retries should not create duplicate product identities. * **Preserve separation:** The system should preserve marketplace-specific data without polluting the canonical product with marketplace-only fields. ## 25\. Open Product Decisions to Lock Before Implementation Decision Recommended V1 Decision to Discuss **Exact marketplace launch order** Pick 2–3 marketplaces for first production validation; add adapters incrementally. **Seller input method** Start with guided form + spreadsheet upload; add connected PIM/ERP after core workflow is stable. **Human approval** Default to autonomous submission after validation, with optional approval mode for cautious sellers. **Content language** Start with English; keep the content model language-ready. **Image generation** Do not make image generation a dependency for V1 listing completion. **Marketplace schema refresh** Treat schema/rules as versioned and refreshable rather than static. **Error library** Build an internal error taxonomy and continuously map marketplace errors into it. **Confidence threshold** Define which attributes can be inferred and which always require evidence/confirmation. **Bulk listing** Design for one SKU and bulk SKU jobs from the same underlying workflow. ## 26\. Reference Basis The product requirements above are intentionally marketplace-agnostic. The following official sources were used to ground the marketplace/compliance sections and should be treated as external references, not as permanent hard-coded requirements: * **Amazon Selling Partner API — Product Type Definitions / Retrieve a Product Type Definition:** [https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/lang-en\_EN/docs/retrieve-a-product-type-definition](https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/lang-en_EN/docs/retrieve-a-product-type-definition) * **Amazon Selling Partner API — Manage Product Listings:** [https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/lang-en\_EN/docs/manage-product-listings-guide](https://developer-docs.amazon.com/sp-api/lang-en_EN/docs/manage-product-listings-guide) * **Amazon India Seller Central — apparel image guidance / seller listing guidance:** [https://sellercentral.amazon.in/](https://sellercentral.amazon.in/) * **Flipkart Seller API — Listing Management API:** [https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/listing-api-docs/LMAPIOverview.html](https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/listing-api-docs/LMAPIOverview.html) * **Flipkart Seller API — Marketplace platform overview:** [https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/FMPlatOverview.html](https://seller.flipkart.com/api-docs/FMPlatOverview.html) * **Department of Consumer Affairs, Government of India — Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Third Amendment Rules, 2022:** [https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/legalmetrologyactsandrules/legal-metrology-packaged-commodities-third-amendment-rules-2022](https://consumeraffairs.nic.in/legalmetrologyactsandrules/legal-metrology-packaged-commodities-third-amendment-rules-2022) * **Nykaa Seller Portal — Terms and Conditions / product content and description listing guidelines:** [https://seller.nykaa.com/terms-and-conditions](https://seller.nykaa.com/terms-and-conditions) ### Final Product Principle UNDERSTAND PRODUCT → CLASSIFY → EXTRACT ATTRIBUTES → BUILD CANONICAL PRODUCT → FILL MARKETPLACE SCHEMA → GENERATE CONTENT → VALIDATE → FIND MISSING DATA → ASK HUMAN ONLY WHEN NECESSARY → SUBMIT → CHECK STATUS → FIX ERRORS → RESUBMIT → CONFIRM LIVE → SHOW STATUS.

Founder's Direct POVDocument Status: V1 Product / Business Requirements · Apparel Niche

AUTONOMOUS LISTING AGENT

V1 Business Requirements & End-to-End Listing Process (Apparel / Fashion Marketplace Sellers)
Important Notice on Living Marketplace Rules
Marketplace schemas, required fields, allowed values and validation rules change. The product must therefore treat marketplace requirements as living rules rather than a one-time hard-coded field list. Amazon explicitly provides marketplace/ product-type schemas and notes that requirements can change; Flipkart likewise states that listing rules are subject to change.

Purpose of this Document

Define, in non-technical business language, exactly what the product must collect, understand, create, validate, submit, monitor, repair and report when a seller wants to publish an apparel SKU across marketplaces from one dashboard.

ItemDefinition
V1 product promiseSeller gives basic brand + product information once. The agent turns it into marketplace-ready listings and manages the listing lifecycle until the listing is live or a human decision is genuinely required.
Primary nicheApparel / fashion products.
Primary userD2C brands, manufacturers, traders, small sellers and marketplace agencies managing apparel catalogs.
Core outcomeOne product source of truth → marketplace-specific listing → validation → submission → error resolution → live confirmation.
Operating principleDo not ask the seller for information the system can reliably derive, reuse or validate. Ask only when missing information materially blocks a correct listing.

1. Product in One Sentence

"The Autonomous Listing Agent is a listing operations agent, not merely a content generator. It takes a seller's product information and assets, builds a canonical product record, maps that product to each marketplace's category and field structure, generates or transforms listing content, validates completeness and compliance, submits the listing, reads marketplace responses, fixes resolvable errors, asks the seller only for unresolved information, resubmits, and confirms the final live status."

2. The End-to-End Flow

The complete lifecycle from seller onboarding to live verification consists of 19 operational stages:

1
Seller / brand onboarding
Capture stable business, legal, brand & tax identity once
2
Marketplace account connection
Authenticate seller accounts, store IDs & default commercial terms
3
Product intake
Multi-modal ingestion: forms, CSV, ERP, images & size charts
4
Product understanding
Isolate verified factual data from promotional marketing noise
5
Category & sub-category classification
Map gender & apparel type into marketplace taxonomy
6
Attribute extraction & normalization
Normalize fabric, fit, pattern, color, weave & care
7
Canonical Product Intelligence record
Create immutable single source of truth record
8
Marketplace schema mapping
Transform canonical facts into target marketplace schemas
9
Content generation & optimization
Generate titles, bullets, descriptions & search keywords
10
Media and variant validation
Validate size charts, swatch shots, parent-child links
11
Compliance & completeness validation
Pre-flight checks against Legal Metrology 2022 & portal rules
12
Human clarification only where necessary
Targeted single-question prompts for blocking gaps
13
Marketplace submission
Dispatch validated payloads to marketplace APIs
14
Submission/status monitoring
Asynchronous polling & webhook listeners for feed outcomes
15
Error diagnosis
Translate raw portal error codes into plain actionable language
16
Automatic correction
Auto-fix deterministic enum mismatches, formatting & sizing
17
Resubmission
Safe bounded retry with updated payload and incremented attempt
18
Live confirmation
Capture live URL, marketplace SKU, ASIN/FSN and active state
19
Dashboard status + audit history
Show unified multi-marketplace operational view & audit trail

3. V1 Scope and Non-Goals

Definition of Success
A product is not considered 'listed' merely because a submission was sent. It is successful only when the marketplace confirms the relevant SKU/listing is live/active and the dashboard can show the marketplace identifier, current status and latest validation state.
In V1 ScopeNot the Primary V1 Objective
Apparel product listingFull marketplace order management
Multi-marketplace listing from one dashboardFull inventory/warehouse management
Product/category/attribute understandingAdvertising optimization
Title, bullets, description, keywords and structured attributesPricing optimization as a standalone agent
Variant and media handlingReturns/reconciliation as a standalone workflow
Validation, error interpretation and correctionCustomer service automation
Listing status and historyEnd-to-end marketplace business operating system

4. Marketplace Strategy

V1 should be designed around a common apparel product model plus marketplace-specific adapters. The common model is the source of truth. Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are required, optional, conditionally required, allowed values, formatting rules, variation rules and submission/status behavior.

  • Target marketplace set: Can include Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, AJIO, Meesho and Nykaa Fashion, subject to the commercial/API access available to the business.
  • Category Semantic Variance: Do not assume that the same apparel category means the same thing on every marketplace.
  • No Hard-Coded Lists: Do not hard-code a single universal 'required fields' list.
  • Dynamic Schemas: For each connected marketplace, the product should maintain a current marketplace/category schema and map the canonical product into it.
  • Amazon Documentation: Amazon's current developer documentation describes Product Type Definitions as the source for product-type and marketplace requirements, including required/conditional attributes.
  • Flipkart Documentation: Flipkart's official Listing Management documentation similarly separates product information from the seller listing and states that listing rules can change, so errors should be handled explicitly.

The End-to-End Flow The complete lifecycle from seller onboarding to live verification consists of 19 operational stages: 1 Seller / brand onboarding Capture stable business, legal, brand & tax identity once 2 Marketplace account connection Authenticate seller accounts, store IDs & default commercial terms 3 Product intake Multi-modal ingestion: forms, CSV, ERP, images & size charts 4 Product understanding Isolate verified factual data from promotional marketing noise 5 Category & sub-category classification Map gender & apparel type into marketplace taxonomy 6 Attribute extraction & normalization Normalize fabric, fit, pattern, color, weave & care 7 Canonical Product Intelligence record Create immutable single source of truth record 8 Marketplace schema mapping Transform canonical facts into target marketplace schemas 9 Content generation & optimization Generate titles, bullets, descriptions & search keywords 10 Media and variant validation Validate size charts, swatch shots, parent-child links 11 Compliance & completeness validation Pre-flight checks against Legal Metrology 2022 & portal rules 12 Human clarification only where necessary Targeted single-question prompts for blocking gaps 13 Marketplace submission Dispatch validated payloads to marketplace APIs 14 Submission/status monitoring Asynchronous polling & webhook listeners for feed outcomes 15 Error diagnosis Translate raw portal error codes into plain actionable language 16 Automatic correction Auto-fix deterministic enum mismatches, formatting & sizing 17 Resubmission Safe bounded retry with updated payload and incremented attempt 18 Live confirmation Capture live URL, marketplace SKU, ASIN/FSN and active state 19 Dashboard status + audit history Show unified multi-marketplace operational view & audit trail ## 3\. V1 Scope and Non-Goals Definition of Success A product is not considered 'listed' merely because a submission was sent. It is successful only when the marketplace confirms the relevant SKU/listing is live/active and the dashboard can show the marketplace identifier, current status and latest validation state. In V1 Scope Not the Primary V1 Objective Apparel product listing Full marketplace order management Multi-marketplace listing from one dashboard Full inventory/warehouse management Product/category/attribute understanding Advertising optimization Title, bullets, description, keywords and structured attributes Pricing optimization as a standalone agent Variant and media handling Returns/reconciliation as a standalone workflow Validation, error interpretation and correction Customer service automation Listing status and history End-to-end marketplace business operating system ## 4\. Marketplace Strategy V1 should be designed around a common apparel product model plus marketplace-specific adapters. The common model is the source of truth. Each marketplace adapter decides which fields are required, optional, conditionally required, allowed values, formatting rules, variation rules and submission/status behavior. * **Target marketplace set:** Can include **Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, AJIO, Meesho and Nykaa Fashion**, subject to the commercial/API access available to the business. * **Category Semantic Variance:** Do not assume that the same apparel category means the same thing on every marketplace. * **No Hard-Coded Lists:** Do not hard-code a single universal 'required fields' list. * **Dynamic Schemas:** For each connected marketplace, the product should maintain a current marketplace/category schema and map the canonical product into it. * **Amazon Documentation:** Amazon's current developer documentation describes Product Type Definitions as the source for product-type and marketplace requirements, including required/conditional attributes. * **Flipkart Documentation:** Flipkart's official Listing Management documentation similarly separates product information from the seller listing and states that listing rules can change, so errors should be handled explicitly. ```mermaid graph LR CP["Canonical Apparel Model

pages.title: 45-Day Plan & Definition of Done
pages.description: Executive overview of the 45-Day MVP Build Plan (GCP Edition) for the AI Marketplace OS. Kickoff context, Day-45 Definition of Done, 10 Non-Negotiable Invariants, and the core operational loop.
pages.html:
Executive Summary & Timeline

The AI Marketplace OS 45-Day MVP Build Plan (GCP Edition) outlines an aggressive, production-ready roadmap to build and launch an AI-powered marketplace listing operator for D2C brands across Amazon and Flipkart.

The plan is built around a realistic constraint: you build the foundational architecture solo for ~10 days, then onboard 4 engineers (5-person team total) to scale out into full speed.

Sprint Duration
45 Calendar Days
Mon Sep 21, 2026 → Wed Nov 4, 2026
Team Model
1 Solo → 5 People
10-day foundation sprint, then 35 days scaled
Cloud Platform
Google Cloud (GCP)
Cloud Run, Cloud SQL pgvector, Redis, KMS
Launch Scope
Amazon + Flipkart
LWA SP-API & Flipkart Seller API adapters

Day-45 Definition of Done

On Day 45, a real D2C brand user must be able to perform the complete journey end-to-end in production without any manual engineering intervention:

  • Sign in & Tenant Isolation: Sign in securely via JWT, select a brand, and maintain 100% tenant-scoped data isolation.
  • Marketplace OAuth: Connect an Amazon and/or Flipkart account via OAuth with credentials encrypted at rest.
  • Product Import: Import products via CSV (bulk) or manual entry with automated validation and image upload to GCS.
  • AI Listing Generation: Trigger AI generation for title, bullets, description, keywords, and attributes conditioned on the brand's voice guide via pgvector RAG.
  • Deterministic & Vision Validation: View deterministic rule failures and vision-based image compliance issues formatted as unified, structured errors.
  • Bounded Self-Correction: Watch the system automatically repair field-level errors (max 3 retries) and block gracefully when human intervention is needed.
  • Maker-Checker Approval: Review listings side-by-side per marketplace, edit fields, and approve or reject with audit trail (creator cannot approve own listing).
  • Marketplace Publishing: Publish approved listings via marketplace adapters with per-field success/failure reporting and live operational analytics.

10 Non-Negotiable Architectural Invariants

These 10 invariants are non-negotiable for the entire 45 days and beyond. Under deadline pressure, no engineer is permitted to cut corners on these rules:

Non-Negotiable Architecture Invariants
  1. AI never publishes directly: Only adapters publish, and strictly after human approval.
  2. Rules Engine is deterministic code: It is never an LLM call; rules are deterministic code and the final arbiter.
  3. Human approval is mandatory in MVP: There is zero unvetted auto-publishing in Phase 1.
  4. Marketplace logic stays inside adapters: The canonical listing model never contains marketplace-specific schema structures.
  5. Mandatory tenant isolation on every query: tenant_id scoping is enforced at the repository base class, with zero exceptions.
  6. Marketplace credentials never enter LLM prompts: Tokens are encrypted at rest with Cloud KMS and kept strictly isolated from AI contexts.
  7. Observable AgentRuns: Every generation call persists an AgentRun record logging model, token usage, cost, duration, and status.
  8. Unified ErrorReport shape: Rules engine, vision model, and marketplace API failures all return the exact same structured error contract.
  9. Bounded retries (max 3): Agent correction loops are capped at 3 attempts; no infinite loops ever exist.
  10. Idempotent mutations & partial retries: Partial marketplace failures retry only the specific failed field, never the entire listing.

Core Operational Loop

This is the core operational loop repeated to the team at every standup:

Core Execution Rhythm
AI proposes → Deterministic rules validate → Humans approve → Adapters execute → Performance feeds back

Kickoff Constraints & Solo Phase

During the first 10 days, you build solo. You do not build broad; you build a razor-thin vertical slice that validates the architecture: one category, one marketplace's rules, and one end-to-end AI call. Days 11–14 have a 4-day slack buffer designed to absorb any solo slippage before full-throttle scaling.

pages.title: System Overview
pages.description: Complete platform overview — an AI-powered marketplace listing operator for D2C brands. Understand the four-layer architecture, core design principles, and how every component communicates.
pages.html:
What Is It

The AI Marketplace OS is an AI-powered marketplace listing operator for D2C brands. The platform lets brands create, validate, and publish product listings across multiple marketplaces through a single interface — with AI assistance at every step.

Instead of manually writing titles, bullet points, descriptions, keywords, and attributes for each marketplace — and then reformatting for each platform's rules — the system uses specialized AI agents to generate marketplace-optimized content while preserving the brand's voice and ensuring compliance with each marketplace's specific requirements.

MVP Marketplaces
Amazon + Flipkart
Two adapters proving the adapter pattern generalizes
AI Agents
6 Specialized
Content, Keyword, Attribute, Image, Brand Voice, Optimization
Architecture
4-Layer Platform
Experience → Intelligence → Control → Execution
Data Model
Canonical + Adapters
Marketplace-independent core, marketplace-specific mapping

Core Design Principle

Architectural Principle
AI proposes → Deterministic rules validate → Humans approve → Adapters execute → Performance feeds back

This principle is the foundation of the entire system. AI is never given direct publish authority. Every AI-generated output passes through deterministic validation (Rules Engine), then human review, before any marketplace adapter executes the publish operation. This separation ensures:

  • Safety — No hallucinated content reaches customers without human validation
  • Compliance — Marketplace rules are enforced deterministically, not probabilistically
  • Trust — Brands maintain full control over what goes live
  • Improvement — Performance data feeds back to improve future generations

Four-Layer Architecture

Architecture Diagram: Four-Layer Platform Architecture

graph TB
  subgraph EXP["EXPERIENCE LAYER"]
    direction LR
    E1["Next.js Dashboard"]
    E2["Connect Marketplaces"]
    E3["Import Products"]
    E4["Review & Approve"]
    E5["Analytics"]
  end
  subgraph INT["INTELLIGENCE LAYER"]
    direction LR
    I1["Content Agent"]
    I2["Keyword Agent"]
    I3["Attribute Agent"]
    I4["Image Agent"]
    I5["Brand Voice Retrieval"]
    I6["Optimization Agent"]
  end
  subgraph CTR["CONTROL LAYER"]
    direction LR
    C1["Rules Engine"]
    C2["Structured Errors"]
    C3["Validation"]
    C4["Human Approval Gate"]
  end
  subgraph EXE["EXECUTION LAYER"]
    direction LR
    X1["Amazon SP-API Adapter"]
    X2["Flipkart Seller API Adapter"]
    X3["Canonical → Marketplace Mapping"]
  end
  EXP --> INT
  INT --> CTR
  CTR --> EXE
  EXE -->|"Performance Data"| INT
LayerResponsibilityComponents
ExperienceUser-facing dashboardNext.js app for connect, import, review, approve, analytics
IntelligenceAI generation & retrievalLangGraph agents for content, keywords, attributes, images, brand-voice
ControlDeterministic validation & approvalRules engine, structured error contracts, human approval gate
ExecutionMarketplace operationsAmazon SP-API + Flipkart Seller API adapters

System Flow

The complete data flow from a brand entering the system to a listing appearing on a marketplace follows this path:

Brand (D2C Owner)
↓
Marketplace Accounts (Amazon, Flipkart)
↓
Product Catalog (CSV / Manual / Sync)
↓
Canonical Product Representation
↓
AI Context Assembly (Brand Voice + Rules + Category)
↓
AI Agents (Content + Keyword + Attribute + Image)
↓
Canonical Listing (JSON Schema)
↓
Rules Engine (Deterministic Validation)
↓
Vision Validation (Image Compliance)
↓
Quality / Confidence Scoring
↓
Human Approval Gate
↓
Marketplace Adapter (Amazon SP-API / Flipkart)
↓
Live Marketplace Listing
↓
Performance Data (CTR, Conversions, Returns)
↓
Optimization Agent (Feedback Loop)

Why This Architecture

Why Separate Intelligence, Control, and Execution?

Intelligence (AI agents) is probabilistic — it generates high-quality content but can hallucinate, violate marketplace rules, or drift from brand voice. Control (Rules Engine) is deterministic — it catches violations with certainty. Execution (Adapters) is marketplace-specific — it handles the complexity of each platform's API, auth, and rate limits.

Separating these concerns means:

  • You can change AI models without touching marketplace logic
  • You can add a new marketplace without modifying AI agents
  • You can update rules without redeploying agents
  • Each layer can be tested, monitored, and scaled independently

Why AI Must Not Directly Publish

LLMs are powerful but non-deterministic. A language model might generate a title that violates Amazon's 200-character limit, include a medical claim that regulatory compliance forbids, or use a competitor's trademarked term. Deterministic validation between AI and execution ensures that:

  • Every character count is checked programmatically, not probabilistically
  • Banned terms are caught before they reach the marketplace
  • Category-specific attribute schemas are validated against known templates
  • Image compliance is verified through both pixel analysis and vision models
Architectural Invariant
AI never directly publishes data to any marketplace. The Rules Engine is deterministic. Human approval is required in MVP. These constraints are non-negotiable.

Non-Technical Explanation

Non-Technical Explanation
Think of the system as having an AI writing assistant, a strict quality checker, a human reviewer, and a publishing service — working in sequence. The AI writes the listing content using the brand's voice and marketplace rules. The quality checker catches any violations or errors using strict, programmable rules (not AI). A human then reviews and approves. Only after approval does the system push the listing to Amazon or Flipkart. If the listing performs well, the system learns from that success for future listings.

AI Implementation Context

AI Implementation Context

What an AI coding agent must know before modifying this module:

  • The four-layer separation is an architectural invariant — do not merge layers
  • All AI output must pass through the Rules Engine before human approval
  • The canonical listing model is marketplace-independent
  • Marketplace-specific logic lives exclusively in adapters
  • Performance data flows back to the Intelligence layer, not directly to Execution

What this module must never do:

  • Allow AI agents to bypass the Control layer
  • Put marketplace-specific fields in the canonical model
  • Allow the Experience layer to call marketplace APIs directly
  • Remove human approval in MVP

pages.title: Architecture Principles
pages.description: The foundational principles that guide every architectural decision in the platform. These principles are invariants — they should never be violated.
pages.html:
Core Principles

Primary Principle
AI proposes → Deterministic rules validate → Humans approve → Adapters execute → Performance feeds back into optimization

Every system design decision must align with these principles:

1. AI Is Advisory, Not Authoritative

AI agents generate content suggestions. They never have direct publish authority. All AI output is treated as a proposal that must pass through deterministic validation and human approval before reaching any marketplace.

2. Deterministic Rules Are the Final Arbiter

The Rules Engine enforces marketplace constraints with certainty. No LLM output ships without passing it. Rules are programmable, versioned, and marketplace-specific. They catch what AI misses — character limits, banned terms, missing attributes, image specifications.

3. Marketplace Independence via Canonical Model

The core listing representation is marketplace-agnostic. Amazon-specific fields, Flipkart-specific formats, and future marketplace requirements live inside their respective adapters. The canonical model never contains raw marketplace API structures.

4. Adapter Pattern for Marketplace Operations

Every marketplace interaction happens through a well-defined adapter interface. Adding Myntra or Ajio later requires building a new adapter — not rewriting the core platform. Adapters own: auth refresh, rate limiting, idempotency, and error mapping.

5. Tenant Isolation Is Mandatory

Every database query, every API call, every agent run is scoped to a tenant. Cross-tenant data leakage is a critical security violation. Tenant filtering is enforced at the repository layer, not at the application layer.

6. Structured Errors Everywhere

Every failure — rules engine, vision model, marketplace API — returns the same structured ErrorReport envelope. This enables AI correction agents, UI display, logging, retry logic, and debugging from a single contract.

7. Bounded Retries

All retry loops are bounded (max 3 for agent corrections). The system never enters infinite retry loops. Failed jobs surface exact reasons for human intervention.

8. Observability by Default

Every AgentRun records: model_used, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost, duration, status. Every marketplace call is logged. Every validation run is persisted. This creates a complete audit trail and cost observability.

Architectural Invariants

Never Violate These Rules
  1. AI never directly publishes to marketplaces
  2. Rules Engine is deterministic — never an LLM
  3. Human approval is required in MVP
  4. Marketplace-specific logic belongs inside adapters only
  5. Canonical listing model is marketplace-independent
  6. Tenant isolation is mandatory on every query
  7. Marketplace credentials are encrypted at rest (AES-256)
  8. All AgentRuns are observable and persisted
  9. All failures use structured ErrorReport contracts
  10. Retries are bounded (max 3 for agent corrections)
  11. Marketplace mutations are idempotent
  12. Failed fields are retried individually, not the entire listing
  13. Optimization Agent runs on schedule, not continuously
  14. Future marketplaces don't require rewriting the core system

Why These Principles Matter

  • Reliability — LLM can never bypass the Rules Engine; structured errors make every failure actionable
  • Defensibility — Brand-voice vectors + version history + performance feedback loop compound over time
  • Marketplace independence — Canonical model + adapters; adding Myntra/Ajio later is an adapter, not a rewrite
  • Cost efficiency — Event-driven generation (only when needed), model routing, and the optimization agent only fires on schedule, not continuously

LevelExampleRule

Core Variation Invariants
