After 3 failed correction attempts, the job status becomes `BLOCKED`. The exact ErrorReport is surfaced to the user with all failed fields, error codes, and suggestions. The user can then manually edit and resubmit, or provide additional instructions for regeneration.

pages.title: Content Agent
pages.description: The Content Agent generates marketplace-optimized titles, bullet points, and descriptions while maintaining brand voice and preventing hallucinations.
pages.html:
Purpose

The Content Agent is the highest-token-spend agent. It generates the primary text content for marketplace listings: title, bullet points, and description. It must balance marketplace SEO optimization with brand voice adherence, while never fabricating factual product claims.

Default Model
GPT-4o mini
Strong structured output + JSON mode
Token Spend
Highest of all agents
~2000-4000 tokens per generation
Scope
MVP
Core agent in Phase 1

Inputs & Outputs

InputSourcePurpose
Product dataProduct tableSKU, raw title, images, attributes — source of truth for factual claims
Brand voice chunkspgvector retrievalTone, style, glossary, compliance rules
Marketplace rulesRules tableCharacter limits, banned terms, required attributes in title
Category templateCategory mappingCategory-specific content expectations
Approved examplesListingVersion tablePreviously approved listings for reference

Outputs: Title, bullet points (array), description — as structured JSON matching the output schema.

Prompt Construction

Content Agent System Prompt
You are a marketplace listing specialist for {marketplace}.
Generate a product title, {num_bullets} bullet points, and a description.

RULES (NON-NEGOTIABLE):
- Title: ≤ {max_title_length} characters
- Each bullet: ≤ {max_bullet_length} characters  
- Description: ≤ {max_desc_length} characters
- BANNED TERMS: {banned_terms_list}
- Title MUST include: Brand name, product type, key differentiator

BRAND VOICE:
{brand_voice_chunks}

PRODUCT DATA (factual source of truth):
SKU: {sku}
Raw Title: {raw_title}
Category: {category}
Material: {material}
Color: {color}
Attributes: {attributes_json}

DO NOT invent materials, certifications, measurements, medical claims,
or specifications not present in the product data above.

Respond with JSON: { "title": "...", "bullets": [...], "description": "..." }

Hallucination Control

Factual Accuracy
The Content Agent separates factual claims from creative language. It MUST NOT invent:
  • Materials or fabric compositions
  • Certifications (organic, BIS, ISO)
  • Measurements or dimensions
  • Medical or health claims
  • Performance claims or guarantees
  • Product specifications not in the source data
The Rules Engine cross-references generated claims against the product record.

Example Request/Response

Content Agent Output
{
  "title": "Fabrica Organic Cotton Kurta Set for Women | Navy Blue | Handloom Weave | Sizes XS-XXL",
  "bullets": [
    "Crafted from 100% organic cotton certified by GOTS for breathable all-day comfort",
    "Traditional handloom weave with contemporary silhouette — pairs effortlessly for festive or everyday wear",
    "Set includes full-length kurta and matching palazzo pants with elasticated waist",
    "Machine washable at 30°C — retains colour vibrancy wash after wash",
    "Available in sizes XS through XXL with detailed size guide for perfect fit"
  ],
  "description": "Elevate your ethnic wardrobe with the Fabrica Organic Cotton Kurta Set..."
}

Engineering Implementation

Content Agent Pseudocode
class ContentAgent:
    def __init__(self, model_router, prompt_builder):
        self.model_router = model_router
        self.prompt_builder = prompt_builder
    
    async def generate(self, context: AgentContext) -> ContentOutput:
        # 1. Build prompt with brand voice + rules
        prompt = self.prompt_builder.build_content_prompt(context)
        
        # 2. Select model via router
        model = self.model_router.select(
            task="content_generation",
            marketplace=context.marketplace,
            complexity=context.complexity_score
        )
        
        # 3. Call model with JSON mode
        response = await model.generate(
            messages=prompt.messages,
            response_format=ContentOutputSchema,
            temperature=0.7
        )
        
        # 4. Validate structured output
        output = ContentOutputSchema.model_validate_json(response)
        
        return output
Non-Technical Explanation
The Content Agent is like a skilled copywriter who knows your brand's voice, understands each marketplace's requirements, and never makes up product facts. It reads your product data, studies your brand's writing style, checks the marketplace's rules, and writes optimized titles, bullet points, and descriptions — all while staying factually accurate.

pages.html:
Purpose

The Keyword Agent generates discovery-optimized search terms and backend keywords. It focuses on what shoppers actually search for, not keyword stuffing. Backend keywords (Amazon-specific) are terms that don't appear in the listing but help with search visibility.

Inputs & Outputs

InputSource
CategoryCategory mapping
Product attributesProduct table
MarketplaceTarget marketplace
Existing search signalsPerformance data (Phase 3)
Brand terminologyBrand glossary chunks

Output: search_terms (array), backend_keywords (array), keyword_recommendations (optional).

Validation Rules

  • No keyword stuffing — each term must be semantically distinct
  • Backend keywords must not duplicate visible listing content (Amazon rule)
  • No competitor brand names in keywords
  • Marketplace-specific keyword length limits respected
  • Amazon backend keyword limit: 250 bytes total
Non-Technical Explanation
The Keyword Agent figures out what words shoppers use to find products like yours. It generates search-friendly terms without stuffing irrelevant keywords — because marketplaces penalize that. Think of it as an SEO specialist who knows exactly how Amazon and Flipkart search works.

pages.html:
Purpose

The Attribute Agent converts product information into marketplace-specific structured attributes. Each marketplace has its own category schema with different attribute names, allowed values, and requirements.

Marketplace Mapping Example

CanonicalAmazonFlipkart
color = "navy blue"Color = "Navy"Colour = "Navy Blue"
material = "organic cotton"Material = "Cotton"Fabric = "Organic Cotton"
size = "L"Size = "Large"Size = "L"

Engineering Notes

Architecture Decision
Marketplace-specific attribute mapping belongs inside marketplace adapters / mapping layers — NOT spread throughout the AI system. The Attribute Agent generates canonical attributes; the adapter maps them to marketplace-specific formats. This keeps marketplace logic contained.

Missing attributes are flagged in the ErrorReport with source "rules_engine" and error code "MISSING_ATTRIBUTE". Category mismatch (product doesn't fit the selected category schema) is flagged as "CATEGORY_MISMATCH".

pages.title: Optimization Agent
pages.description: The Optimization Agent analyzes performance data and proposes improvements to existing listings. Runs on schedule, not continuously.
pages.html:
Purpose

The Optimization Agent consumes performance metrics (impressions, clicks, conversions, returns, ranking) and proposes changes to existing listings. It identifies underperforming listings, analyzes patterns in high-performing listings, and suggests specific field-level improvements.

Trigger Model

Scheduled, Not Continuous
The Optimization Agent runs on a schedule (e.g., weekly), not continuously. It fires on a schedule, analyzes accumulated performance data, and generates optimization proposals. This is critical for cost efficiency — continuous optimization would be expensive and unnecessary.

Input: Performance metrics per listing per marketplace. Output: Proposed changes to existing listings (title, bullets, keywords). These proposals go through the same validation → approval pipeline as new listings.

pages.title: Future Agent Registry
pages.description: How new agents can be registered and integrated into the platform without rewriting core infrastructure.
pages.html:
Registry Design

The agent registry pattern allows new agents to be added without modifying the core orchestration layer. Each agent implements a standard interface:

class AgentInterface(ABC):
    """Standard interface for all agents."""
    name: str
    version: str
    scope: str  # "mvp" | "phase2" | "phase3" | "future"
    
    @abstractmethod
    async def execute(self, context: AgentContext) -> AgentOutput: ...
    
    @abstractmethod
    def get_input_schema(self) -> dict: ...
    
    @abstractmethod
    def get_output_schema(self) -> dict: ...

New agents register with the orchestrator and plug into the existing data layer, validation pipeline, and observability infrastructure. This is how the Listing Agent can expand into the full Marketplace OS without platform rewrites.

pages.title: Image Compliance Pipeline
pages.description: The complete image compliance pipeline — from upload through deterministic checks, vision model analysis, to structured ImageReport.
pages.html:
Why a Dedicated Pipeline

Amazon and Flipkart reject listings silently or visibly for image violations — white-background rules, resolution, text overlays, watermarks. This pipeline runs before human approval, in parallel with text generation. Catching image issues early prevents wasted publishing attempts.

Pipeline Flow

Architecture Diagram: Image Compliance Pipeline

graph TD
  UP["Image Upload"] --> S3["Store in S3"]
  S3 --> DET["Deterministic Checks"]
  DET -->|"resolution, format, aspect ratio, EXIF"| VIS["Vision Model Review"]
  VIS -->|"background, fill, text, watermark"| RPT["Structured ImageReport"]
  RPT --> CHECK{"Pass/Warn/Fail?"}
  CHECK -->|"Pass"| ATTACH["Attach to listing"]
  CHECK -->|"Fail/Warn"| FEEDBACK["Surface issue + suggested fix"]
  FEEDBACK --> USER["User reviews"]
  USER -->|"Fix & re-upload"| UP
  USER -->|"Accept warning"| ATTACH

Architecture

Marketplace-specific rules are stored as policy configurations — NOT hardcoded into the vision agent. Amazon and Flipkart image rules are separate policy documents that the pipeline evaluates against. This means adding a new marketplace's image rules requires only a new policy configuration, not code changes.

Invariant
Marketplace image rules are policy configurations, not hardcoded logic. The vision agent evaluates images against loaded policies.

pages.title: Image Processing Flow
pages.description: Detailed step-by-step image processing from upload to final report.
pages.html:
Processing Steps

  1. Image uploaded via API → stored in S3 with tenant-scoped path
  2. File validation: format (JPEG/PNG/TIFF), corruption check, EXIF extraction
  3. Deterministic checks: resolution, aspect ratio, dimensions, file size
  4. Vision model analysis: background color, product fill ratio, text overlays, watermarks, logo placement
  5. Marketplace rule evaluation: check results against marketplace-specific policies
  6. Generate structured ImageReport with per-check results
  7. Return pass/warn/fail with suggestions for each issue

pages.title: Vision Model Checks
pages.description: Vision model analysis for image compliance — background, product fill, text overlays, watermarks.
pages.html:
Vision Model Checks

Using GPT-4o-mini (vision), the system analyzes each image for:

  • Background compliance — Is the background pure white (Amazon) or light (Flipkart)?
  • Product fill ratio — Does the product fill ≥85% of the frame (Amazon)?
  • Text overlays — Any text detected on the main image?
  • Watermarks — Any visible watermarks?
  • Logo placement — Only product logo on the product itself?
  • Product visibility — Is the product clearly visible and well-lit?

The vision model returns structured findings that are evaluated against marketplace-specific policies.

pages.title: Brand Voice Architecture
pages.description: Complete brand voice architecture — vectorization, chunking, embedding, retrieval, and context injection into AI agents.
pages.html:
Architecture Overview

Brand intelligence ensures that AI-generated content sounds like the brand, not like generic AI output. The system stores pieces of the brand's writing style, terminology, and compliance rules as vector embeddings, then retrieves the most relevant pieces when generating new listings.

Architecture Diagram: Brand Voice Architecture

graph TD
  GUIDE["Brand Voice Guide"] --> CHUNK["Chunking"]
  STYLE["Style Guide"] --> CHUNK
  GLOSS["Glossary"] --> CHUNK
  APPROVE["Approved Listings"] --> CHUNK
  COMPLY["Compliance Rules"] --> CHUNK
  CHUNK --> EMBED["Embedding: text-embedding-3-small"]
  EMBED --> STORE["pgvector Storage"]
  STORE --> RETRIEVE["Cosine Similarity Retrieval"]
  RETRIEVE --> PROMPT["Inject into Agent Prompt"]

Retrieval Flow

At generation time: embed the request context ("women's ethnic wear, brand X, tone: playful") → pgvector cosine-similarity search over brand embeddings (top-k = 8) → inject retrieved chunks as "Brand Voice Context" in the agent prompt.

Non-Technical Explanation
The system stores pieces of the brand's writing style and finds the most relevant pieces whenever it writes a new listing. This ensures the AI always sounds like the brand.

pages.title: Vector Retrieval
pages.description: How pgvector cosine similarity retrieval works at generation time.
pages.html:
Retrieval Process

graph LR
  Q["Query: product + brand + marketplace + tone"] --> EMB["Embed query"]
  EMB --> PGV["pgvector cosine-similarity: top-k=8"]
  PGV --> FILTER["Filter by relevance threshold"]
  FILTER --> CTX["Brand Voice Context for prompt"]

Why pgvector

  • One database for relational data AND embeddings
  • Zero extra operational surface for MVP
  • Cosine similarity via <=> operator sufficient at this scale (thousands of chunks, not millions)
  • Migrate to dedicated vector store only if retrieval latency demands it

pages.title: Marketplace Abstraction
pages.description: How marketplace differences are abstracted behind a unified interface.
pages.html:
Marketplace Abstraction

The rest of the system never touches raw marketplace APIs. All marketplace interaction happens through the adapter interface. The canonical model is the boundary — everything above it is marketplace-independent, everything below it is marketplace-specific. This clean separation means adding a new marketplace is an adapter, not a rewrite.
pages.markdown:
## Marketplace Abstraction

The rest of the system never touches raw marketplace APIs. All marketplace interaction happens through the adapter interface. The canonical model is the boundary — everything above it is marketplace-independent, everything below it is marketplace-specific. This clean separation means adding a new marketplace is an adapter, not a rewrite.

Invariant

pages.title: Marketplace Adapter Pattern
pages.description: The adapter pattern for marketplace operations — interface, responsibilities, and implementation guide.
pages.html:
Adapter Interface

MarketplaceAdapter ABC
class MarketplaceAdapter(ABC):
    async def get_listing(self, sku) -> ListingResult
    async def create_listing(self, listing) -> ListingResult
    async def update_listing(self, listing) -> ListingResult
    async def publish_listing(self, listing) -> ListingResult
    async def get_performance(self, listing_id, from_date, to_date) -> PerformanceResult

Adapter Responsibilities

  • Every method returns ListingResult with per-field success/failure, not a boolean
  • On partial success, return exactly which fields failed + marketplace's raw error string
  • Adapters own: auth refresh, rate limiting, idempotency, error mapping to unified ErrorReport
  • Canonical model → marketplace-specific mapping happens inside the adapter
  • The rest of the system never touches raw marketplace APIs
pages.markdown:

pages.title: Amazon Adapter
pages.description: Amazon SP-API adapter — authentication, listing operations, rate limiting, and error mapping.
pages.html:
Authentication

Amazon SP-API uses OAuth 2.0 with LWA (Login with Amazon). The adapter manages: initial OAuth flow, token storage (AES-256 encrypted), automatic token refresh, and expiration handling. If refresh fails, escalate to user.

Operations

graph LR
  CAN["Canonical Listing"] --> MAP["Field Mapping"]
  MAP --> AMZ["Amazon SP-API Call"]
  AMZ --> RES["Per-field Response"]
  RES --> RESULT["ListingResult"]

Rate Limiting

Amazon SP-API has per-endpoint rate limits. The adapter implements: request throttling per marketplace account, exponential backoff on 429 responses, and queue-based request scheduling to stay within limits.

pages.title: Future Marketplace Adapter
pages.description: How future marketplace adapters (Myntra, Ajio, Meesho) would be added.
pages.html:
Adding a New Marketplace

To add Myntra, Ajio, or any new marketplace: implement the MarketplaceAdapter interface, create field mapping configuration, define image compliance policy, register marketplace rules, and test. No core platform changes required — this is the power of the adapter pattern.

Non-Technical Explanation
Adding a new marketplace is like adding a new language translator to the team. The core system speaks one "language" (canonical model), and each marketplace adapter translates it into that marketplace's specific format.

pages.title: Marketplace Error Mapping

Each adapter maps marketplace-specific error codes to the unified ErrorReport taxonomy. Example: Amazon's "IMAGE_NOT_COMPLIANT" maps to { field: "main_image", error_code: "API_REJECTED_PARTIAL", source: "amazon_adapter" }. This enables consistent error handling across all marketplaces.

pages.title: Database Schema
pages.description: Complete database schema with all tables, columns, types, and relationships.
pages.html:
Core Schema

Core Tables
-- Tenant / Brand
CREATE TABLE tenants (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  tone TEXT,
  guidelines JSONB,
  glossary JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Brand Chunks (pgvector)
CREATE TABLE brand_chunks (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  brand_id UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  type TEXT NOT NULL, -- tone_rule, glossary, compliance, example
  text TEXT NOT NULL,
  embedding vector(1536),
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Products
CREATE TABLE products (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  brand_id UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  sku TEXT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  images JSONB,
  attributes JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

-- Marketplace Accounts
CREATE TABLE marketplace_accounts (
  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  brand_id UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  marketplace TEXT NOT NULL, -- amazon, flipkart
  token_enc BYTEA NOT NULL, -- AES-256 encrypted
  status TEXT DEFAULT 'active',
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),

  external_id TEXT,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

  id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  product_id UUID REFERENCES products(id),
  trigger TEXT NOT NULL,
  model_used TEXT,
  tokens_in INTEGER,
  tokens_out INTEGER,
  cost DECIMAL(10,6),
  status TEXT NOT NULL,
  error_report_json JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

Unified ErrorReport
{
  "status": "failed",
  "error_code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",
  "retryable": true,
  "attempts_used": 1,
  "max_attempts": 3,
  "errors": [

      "error_code": "TITLE_TOO_LONG",
      "message": "Title is 221 chars; Amazon limit is 200",
      "value_submitted": "Organic Cotton Kurta Set... (221 chars)",
      "suggestion": "Shorten to <= 200 chars; move detail to bullets",
      "source": "rules_engine",
      "retryable": true,
      "marketplace": "amazon"
    }
  ]
}

graph LR

  VALIDATE --> CHECK{"Pass?"}
  CHECK -->|"No"| ERR

pages.title: Async Processing
pages.description: Redis + ARQ architecture for async job processing — why marketplace calls never block HTTP requests.
pages.html:
Why Async

Marketplace API calls are slow (seconds to minutes). AI generation takes 5-30 seconds. Bulk imports process hundreds of products. None of these should block the HTTP request cycle. The async architecture uses Redis as a message broker with ARQ as the task queue framework.

Architecture

graph LR
  API["API Request"] --> JOB["Create Job"]
  JOB --> QUEUE["Redis Queue"]
  QUEUE --> WORKER["ARQ Worker"]
  WORKER --> EXEC["Agent Execution / Adapter Call"]
  EXEC --> DB["Update Database"]
  DB --> UI["UI Status Update"]

The API returns immediately with a job ID (HTTP 202). The client polls for status or receives webhook notifications.

Marketplace API calls are slow (seconds to minutes). AI generation takes 5-30 seconds. Bulk imports process hundreds of products. None of these should block the HTTP request cycle. The async architecture uses Redis as a message broker with ARQ as the task queue framework.

pages.title: Exponential Backoff
pages.description: Exponential backoff implementation for rate-limited marketplace APIs.
pages.html:
Exponential Backoff

For rate-limited responses (HTTP 429): initial delay 1s, multiply by 2 each attempt, add random jitter to prevent thundering herd. Max delay capped at 60s. No agent involvement — purely automatic. This handles Amazon and Flipkart rate limiting gracefully.
pages.markdown:
## Exponential Backoff

For rate-limited responses (HTTP 429): initial delay 1s, multiply by 2 each attempt, add random jitter to prevent thundering herd. Max delay capped at 60s. No agent involvement — purely automatic. This handles Amazon and Flipkart rate limiting gracefully.

pages.title: Rate Limiting
pages.description: Per-marketplace rate limiting to respect API quotas.
pages.html:
Rate Limiting

Each marketplace adapter implements its own rate limiter based on the marketplace's published API quotas. Requests are queued and dispatched within limits. If limits are exceeded, exponential backoff applies. Rate limit metrics are tracked for observability.
pages.markdown:
## Rate Limiting

Each marketplace adapter implements its own rate limiter based on the marketplace's published API quotas. Requests are queued and dispatched within limits. If limits are exceeded, exponential backoff applies. Rate limit metrics are tracked for observability.

pages.title: Marketplace Throttling
pages.description: How marketplace API throttling is managed per-account.
pages.html:
Marketplace Throttling

Bounded concurrency per marketplace account ensures we never exceed API limits. Each marketplace adapter maintains a semaphore/token bucket that controls how many concurrent API calls are in flight. This prevents mass bulk operations from triggering account-level throttling.
pages.markdown:
## Marketplace Throttling

Bounded concurrency per marketplace account ensures we never exceed API limits. Each marketplace adapter maintains a semaphore/token bucket that controls how many concurrent API calls are in flight. This prevents mass bulk operations from triggering account-level throttling.

pages.title: Idempotency
pages.description: Idempotency keys on all marketplace mutations — never double-publish.
pages.html:
Idempotency

Invariant
Marketplace mutations are idempotent. Every marketplace write operation includes an idempotency key. If a network failure causes uncertainty about whether a publish succeeded, retrying with the same key is safe — the marketplace will deduplicate.

pages.title: Partial Failure Handling
pages.description: Handling partial marketplace success — retry only failed fields.
pages.html:
Partial Failure Handling

Invariant
On partial API success, retry only failed fields — never re-push the whole listing. The adapter's ListingResult tells exactly which fields succeeded and which failed. This prevents overwriting already-successful fields and reduces unnecessary API calls.

Invariant

pages.html:
Dead Letter Handling

Jobs that exhaust all retry attempts are moved to a dead letter queue. Each failed job preserves its full ErrorReport, input context, and failure history. Operators can inspect, fix, and resubmit dead-lettered jobs.

Every AgentRun stores its complete input and ErrorReport. Failed jobs can be re-submitted with the same input — the system creates a new AgentRun with the same context. This enables debugging and recovery without data loss.

  2. If output fails JSON validation twice → escalate to next tier (GPT-4o)

  4. Embeddings always use the embedding model; never run generation model for retrieval
  5. Log model_used, tokens, and cost on every AgentRun

pages.title: Heavy Reasoning Escalation
pages.description: When and how to escalate to heavier (more expensive) models for complex corrections.
pages.html:
Escalation Criteria

Escalate to the heavier model only when: JSON output fails validation twice with mini, semantic correction fails repeatedly (same error persists), or the task requires complex multi-constraint reasoning. Escalation is per-agent-run, not global — other agent runs continue with the default model.

  3. Re-prompt with error details and stricter instructions
  4. If still failing, escalate to heavier model

pages.title: AI Cost Optimization
pages.description: Strategies for minimizing AI costs — model routing, caching, avoiding unnecessary regeneration.
pages.html:
Optimization Strategies

  • Model routing — Use cheapest model that meets quality bar
  • Prompt compression — Minimize token usage in prompts
  • Retrieval top-k — Only retrieve most relevant brand chunks (top-k=8)
  • Caching — Cache repeated queries/embeddings
  • Avoid unnecessary regeneration — Don't regenerate if only one field failed
  • Event-driven generation — Generate only when needed, not on schedule
  • Reuse approved outputs — Clone approved listings for similar products
  • Image processing only when required — Skip unchanged images
  • Batch embeddings — Batch embed multiple chunks in one API call
  • Bounded retries — Max 3 correction attempts, not unlimited
pages.markdown:
## Optimization Strategies

*   **Model routing** — Use cheapest model that meets quality bar
*   **Prompt compression** — Minimize token usage in prompts
*   **Retrieval top-k** — Only retrieve most relevant brand chunks (top-k=8)
*   **Caching** — Cache repeated queries/embeddings
*   **Avoid unnecessary regeneration** — Don't regenerate if only one field failed
*   **Event-driven generation** — Generate only when needed, not on schedule
*   **Reuse approved outputs** — Clone approved listings for similar products
*   **Image processing only when required** — Skip unchanged images
*   **Batch embeddings** — Batch embed multiple chunks in one API call
*   **Bounded retries** — Max 3 correction attempts, not unlimited

Invariant

pages.title: Tenant Isolation
pages.description: How tenant data isolation is enforced at the database level.
pages.html:
Tenant Isolation

Repository-level enforcement: every query method includes WHERE tenant_id = :tenant_id. The tenant_id comes from the authenticated JWT — it cannot be overridden by the client. This pattern is implemented in a base repository class that all entity repositories extend.
pages.markdown:
## Tenant Isolation

pages.title: pgvector
pages.description: pgvector extension for vector similarity search in PostgreSQL.
pages.html:
pgvector

The pgvector extension adds vector data types and similarity search operators to PostgreSQL. Used for brand voice retrieval: store 1536-dimensional embeddings, query with cosine similarity (<=> operator). IVFFlat indexing for performance at scale.

Non-Technical Explanation
pgvector lets us store and search through "meaning vectors" — numerical representations of brand writing style — directly in our regular database, without needing a separate specialized database.
pages.markdown:
## pgvector

The pgvector extension adds vector data types and similarity search operators to PostgreSQL. Used for brand voice retrieval: store 1536-dimensional embeddings, query with cosine similarity (`<=>` operator). IVFFlat indexing for performance at scale.

Non-Technical Explanation

pgvector lets us store and search through "meaning vectors" — numerical representations of brand writing style — directly in our regular database, without needing a separate specialized database.

pages.title: Cost Optimization Strategy
pages.description: Strategies for reducing operational costs over time.
pages.html:
Cost Optimization

  • Model routing (cheapest model that meets quality bar)
  • Prompt compression (fewer tokens per request)
  • Caching (avoid re-embedding, re-generating unchanged content)
  • Batch operations (bulk embed, batch process)
  • Right-sizing infrastructure (don't over-provision)
  • Reserved instances for predictable workloads

*   Caching (avoid re-embedding, re-generating unchanged content)

pages.title: QA Checklist
pages.description: QA checklist — test strategy, test cases, and coverage requirements.
pages.html:
QA Checklist

  • Unit tests for all services
  • Integration tests for API endpoints
  • Agent output validation tests
  • Rules engine test cases (invalid title, banned term, missing attribute)
  • Image compliance test cases (invalid image, wrong background, low resolution)
  • Marketplace adapter tests (API failure, rate limit, auth expiry, partial publish)
  • Security tests (tenant isolation, unauthorized access, RBAC)
  • End-to-end tests (full flow from import to publish)
  • Load tests (bulk import, concurrent generation)
  • Failure injection tests (network failure, model timeout, DB failure)

pages.title: Security Checklist
pages.description: Security checklist — encryption, authentication, authorization, audit.
pages.html:
Security Checklist

  • JWT authentication implemented and tested
  • RBAC authorization on all endpoints
  • Maker-checker enforcement verified
  • Tenant isolation tested (cross-tenant data access blocked)
  • Marketplace tokens encrypted (AES-256)
  • Secrets in AWS Secrets Manager
  • TLS on all connections
  • Audit logging for all important actions
  • Input validation on all endpoints
  • SQL injection prevention verified
  • CORS configured correctly

pages.title: Architectural Invariants
pages.description: The non-negotiable architectural rules that must never be violated.
pages.html:
Architectural Invariants

Never Violate These Rules
  1. AI never directly publishes to marketplaces
  2. Rules Engine is deterministic — never an LLM
  3. Human approval is required in MVP
  4. Marketplace-specific logic belongs inside adapters only
  5. Canonical listing model is marketplace-independent
  6. Tenant isolation is mandatory on every query
  7. Marketplace credentials are encrypted at rest (AES-256)
  8. All AgentRuns are observable and persisted
  9. All failures use structured ErrorReport contracts
  10. Retries are bounded (max 3 for agent corrections)
  11. Marketplace mutations are idempotent
  12. Failed fields are retried individually, not the entire listing
  13. Optimization Agent runs on schedule, not continuously
  14. Future marketplaces don't require rewriting the core system

These invariants are the foundation of the system's reliability, security, and extensibility. Any modification to the codebase — by a human or an AI coding agent — must preserve these invariants.

AI Implementation Context
If you are an AI coding agent reading this: these invariants are non-negotiable. Do not bypass the Rules Engine, do not allow direct publishing, do not mix marketplace logic into the canonical model, and do not remove tenant isolation. If you need to change something that appears to conflict with an invariant, escalate to a human architect.
